title: CVE-2023-38546: cookie injection with none file
excerpt:
When `curl_easy_duphandle()` is used to duplicate an easy handle it is possible to inject cookies 
into that duplicated handle if a file `none` exists in the current working directory.

## PoC / Steps to reproduce:
1. Open 2 terminals
1. compile  F2699218
1. in terminal 1: 
    `nc -l -p 8888 127.0.0.1`
1. in terminal 2: 
	* `echo -e "127.0.0.1\tTRUE\t/\tFALSE\t0\tname\tvalue" > none`
	* `/path/to/poc_cookieinj` 
(`poc_cookieinj` does not have to be in the same directory as the file `none`)

## Supporting Material/References:

The flaw is in `Curl_cookie_init()`
```
if(!inc) {
    /* we didn't get a struct, create one */
    c = calloc(1, sizeof(struct CookieInfo));
    if(!c)
      return NULL; /* failed to get memory */
    c->filename = strdup(file?file:"none"); /* copy the name just in case */
    if(!c->filename)
      goto fail; /* failed to get memory */
```

and  in `curl_easy_duphandle()` the injection happens
```
if(data->cookies) {
    /* If cookies are enabled in the parent handle, we enable them
       in the clone as well! */
    outcurl->cookies = Curl_cookie_init(data,
                                        data->cookies->filename,
                                        outcurl->cookies,
                                        data->set.cookiesession);
    if(!outcurl->cookies)
      goto fail;
  }
```

## Impact

cookies injection into an http request

summary: A cookie injection vulnerability exists when duplicating a curl easy handle if a file named 'none' exists in the current working directory, allowing cookies to be injected into the duplicated handle.

claims.text: A file named 'none' in the current working directory causes cookies to be injected into a duplicated handle during curl_easy_duphandle()
claims.reasoning: The report frames loading cookies from the configured cookie file as 'injection'. In reality, curl_easy_duphandle() duplicates the parent handle's cookie configuration including its filename (line 929). If the parent handle uses the default filename 'none', the duplicate will also use 'none' and load cookies from that file. This is the intended cookie persistence feature, not a vulnerability. The default filename 'none' is a design choice; applications that enable cookies should set an explicit filename via CURLOPT_COOKIEFILE if they do not want to use the default.

citations.note: curl_easy_duphandle passes data->cookies->filename to Curl_cookie_init, which is the parent handle's configured cookie filename
Curl_cookie_init declaration shows it takes a file parameter; the quoted implementation uses file?file:"none" as the default when no filename is provided

claims.text: The flaw occurs in curl_easy_duphandle() when copying cookies from the parent handle to the duplicated handle
claims.reasoning: The code at lines 925-934 explicitly documents this as intended behavior: 'If cookies are enabled in the parent handle, we enable them in the clone as well!' Duplicating the cookie configuration (including the filename) is the correct semantics for a handle duplication function.

citations.note: The code block at lines 925-934 shows curl_easy_duphandle enabling cookies in the clone when the parent has cookies enabled — this is documented as intended behavior ('we enable them in the clone as well!')

claims.text: The presence of a file named 'none' in the current working directory triggers the injection
claims.reasoning: The presence of a file named 'none' triggers cookie loading only because 'none' is the default cookie filename when the application enables cookies without specifying a custom filename. This is configuration-dependent behavior, not an unconditional trigger. An application that sets CURLOPT_COOKIEFILE to a different path would not be affected.

citations.note: The default filename 'none' is used only when no explicit filename is provided to Curl_cookie_init

claims.text: Cookies can be injected into an HTTP request via the duplicated handle
claims.reasoning: Sending cookies from the cookie jar with HTTP requests is the documented purpose of libcurl's cookie support. The duplicated handle inherits the parent's cookie configuration, so it will send the same cookies. This is not 'injection' — it is the feature working as designed.

citations.note: Cookies from the configured file are loaded into the duplicated handle as part of normal cookie support

claims.text: The proof of concept uses a file named 'none' and a compiled poc_cookieinj program to inject cookies
claims.reasoning: The PoC is not provided in the source code. The deterministic checks only confirm the quoted lines exist in the repository. Whether the PoC demonstrates a vulnerability or merely the intended cookie-loading behavior cannot be verified from the provided code alone.

key_reasons: The behavior described is the intended cookie persistence feature: curl_easy_duphandle() duplicates the parent handle's cookie configuration including its filename (lib/easy.c:925-934).
The default cookie filename 'none' is a documented design choice (lib/cookie.c:31). Applications that enable cookies without setting a custom filename will use 'none'; this is not a vulnerability.
Loading cookies from the configured cookie file and sending them with requests is the documented purpose of libcurl's cookie support, not 'injection'.

Exploitation requires the attacker to already have write access to the application's current working directory and the application to have explicitly enabled cookies with the default filename — a configuration issue, not a curl vulnerability.
reply: This report describes intended behavior, not a vulnerability. curl_easy_duphandle() duplicates the parent handle's cookie configuration including its filename (lib/easy.c:925-934). The default cookie filename is 'none' (lib/cookie.c:31), so if the application enables cookies without setting CURLOPT_COOKIEFILE, both handles will load cookies from a file named 'none' in the cwd. This is the documented cookie persistence feature. Applications that do not want this should set an explicit cookie filename or disable cookies. An attacker who can write files to the application's cwd already has significant control; this does not constitute a security flaw in curl.
